```mermaid
    L --> B[BudgetLedger + StopRules]
    L --> S[Scheduler]
    L --> ST[Steering]
    D -. seam 1 .-> LLM[(LLMClient)]
    P -. seam 2 .-> LLM
  end
  subgraph Disk [state dir]
    REG[runs/<run_id>/...]
    INB[workers/<id>/inbox]
    WEV[workers/<id>/events.jsonl]
    MEV[master/events.jsonl]
    LK[locks/]
    AP[approvals/]
  end
  subgraph Herdr session
    W1[worker pane w1] --> RS1[run supervisors]
    W2[worker pane w2] --> RS2[run supervisors]
  end
  RS1 --> TR1[trainer processes] --> REG
  RS2 --> TR2[trainer processes] --> REG
  ST -->|inbox file + nudge keys| INB
  ST -->|read pane / send keys| W1 & W2
  W1 & W2 -->|status events| WEV
  O --> REG & WEV
  L --> MEV
  DASH[Dashboard localhost] --> Disk
```

### 3.1 Master (`master/`)
`MasterLoop` (`master/loop.py`) runs a fixed tick, each tick a pure sequence of
phases over on-disk state:

1. **Ingest** new run events, worker events, telemetry lines (incremental, by
   byte offset), approval decisions and the user stop flag.
2. **Reconcile** the registry by folding events, then probe run locks to find
   runs whose supervisor died (status becomes `lost`).
3. **Observe** (`observe/`): per-run `CurveSummary` from telemetry, plus
   tracebacks from `stdout.log` and a tail of each worker pane.
4. **Prune** (`pruning/`): run the pruning pipeline over each live cohort; each
   `PruneVerdict` is written as a master event, then sent to the owning worker
   as a `stop` inbox message.
5. **Budget and stop** (`budget/`): update the `BudgetLedger`; evaluate
   `StopRule`s; on the first that fires, stop launching, drain or stop runs and
   write the finding.
6. **Decide** (`decision/`): when capacity is free and the current round is
   settled, ask the `DecisionEngine` for a `Decision` (launch configs, verify
   seeds, wait, or stop). Proposals are validated against the search space;
   anything that would change training code or exceed a budget becomes a
   pending `ApprovalRequest` instead of an action, and the loop carries on.
7. **Schedule** (`master/scheduler.py`): allocate run IDs, pick a worker and a
   free device for each accepted proposal.
8. **Steer** (`master/steering.py`): write inbox messages and nudge worker
   panes; respect takeover and busy panes.
9. **Report**: append a one-line digest to the master pane and to
   `master/events.jsonl`, which is what the dashboard shows.

Write-ahead rule: every side effect is first recorded as an intent event with a
deterministic ID (for example inbox message `r0003-assign`), then executed
idempotently. A restart replays intents whose effect is missing.

### 3.2 Worker runtime (`worker/`)
A worker is a Herdr pane plus a runtime that drives it:

- `ClaudeCodeRuntime` (default): starts Claude Code in the pane with a generated
  worker brief (`worker/brief.py`) and a narrow tool allowlist (the `autoexp
  worker ...` commands, read-only file tools). On a nudge, the agent runs
  `autoexp worker handle`, investigates crashes it is asked to debug, and reports
  back with `autoexp worker report`. It must not edit training code without an
  approved `code_change` approval.
- `ShellRuntime`: runs `autoexp worker serve`, which loops the same mechanical
  handler without an agent. Used for tests, for deterministic proof runs, and
  when no agent is available.

`autoexp worker handle` (`worker/handler.py`) is the mechanical part both
runtimes share: it reads the inbox in order, launches assigned runs, forwards
stop requests to run supervisors, and acks each message by moving it to
`handled/`.

A worker can execute several runs at once inside its pane's control: each
assigned run gets a **run supervisor** (`worker/supervisor.py`, entry point
`autoexp run-exec <run_id>`), a detached process that holds the run lock and
its device lock for its whole life, spawns the trainer, tees stdout/stderr to
`runs/<run_id>/stdout.log`, polls `runs/<run_id>/control.json` for stop
requests, and writes lifecycle events. Supervisors are detached so a crashed
agent or closed pane does not kill training; the master re-opens a pane for the
same worker ID and the runs carry on.

### 3.3 Trainers (`trainers/`)
Anything that honours the trainer contract (`trainers/base.py`) is a trainer:
it accepts `--run-dir --config --seed --total-steps --device --threads`, writes
telemetry lines to `runs/<run_id>/metrics.jsonl` through `TelemetryWriter`, and
saves checkpoints under `runs/<run_id>/checkpoints/`. v1 ships a CleanRL-style
single-file PPO for Gymnasium `CartPole-v1` (`trainers/ppo_cartpole.py`), CPU
only. Other RL tasks plug in by registering another command in the config.

### 3.4 Telemetry and observability (`telemetry/`, `observe/`)
Telemetry is our own JSONL, one `TelemetryEvent` per line:

| kind | fields |
|---|---|
| `episode` | `return`, `length`, optional `success` |
| `update` | `policy_loss`, `value_loss`, `entropy`, `approx_kl`, `clipfrac`, `grad_norm`, `lr`, `explained_variance`, `sps` |
| `eval` | `mean_return`, `std_return`, `episodes`, `video_path` (null in v1: video seam) |
| `system` | `cpu_percent`, `rss_mb`, `device_util`, `threads` |

`TelemetryReader` tails each file from a stored byte offset and tolerates a
partial last line and malformed lines (counted, not fatal). `summarize()` folds
events into a `CurveSummary` (rolling mean return over the last 100 episodes,
best so far, latest KL/entropy/value loss, NaN seen, throughput, memory). The
`Observer` combines that with crash evidence from `stdout.log` (traceback
detection) and the worker pane tail (`herdr pane read`).

### 3.5 Pruning (`pruning/`)
Each pruner implements `Pruner.evaluate(cohort) -> list[PruneVerdict]`, where a
cohort is the live runs of one round. `PruningPipeline` runs them in configured
order and records every verdict, including `keep`, with its reasoning.

- `DivergencePruner`: NaN/inf in any loss, approx KL above `kl_max` for
  `kl_patience` consecutive updates, value loss above `value_loss_max`.
- `PlateauPruner`: best rolling return improved by less than `min_delta` over
  the last `patience_steps`, after `min_steps`, and the goal not reached.
- `SuccessiveHalvingPruner`: rungs at fractions of the run budget; `sync` mode
  waits until every live run in the cohort passed the rung then keeps the top
  `1/eta`; `async` (ASHA) mode decides as each run reaches a rung against the
  values recorded there so far. `plan_hyperband()` produces Hyperband brackets
  for the decision engine to fill.
- `LLMJudgePruner` (seam 2): sends compact curve summaries and log excerpts to
  the LLM every `every_ticks`; its verdicts pass through the same validation and
  are budget-gated.

### 3.6 Decision engine (`decision/`)
`DecisionEngine.decide(context) -> Decision`. The context holds the search space,
every run's spec and summary, prune history, budgets and the goal.

- `DeterministicDecisionEngine`: if a config solved the goal on fewer than the
  required seeds, propose the missing seeds; if a config holds on all required
  seeds, decide `stop` (goal reached); otherwise mutate the top-k configs inside
  the search space and skip configs already tried.
- `LLMDecisionEngine` (seam 1): builds a prompt, calls the `LLMClient` for
  structured JSON, validates and clamps it with `decision/validate.py`, and on
  any failure falls back to the deterministic engine. The decision records
  which engine produced it and why a fallback happened.

### 3.7 Budgets and stop rules (`budget/`)
`BudgetLedger` meters wall clock, compute seconds (summed trainer process
time), environment steps, LLM calls and LLM cost. Stop rules, first match wins:
goal reached (winner holds on `seeds_required` seeds), wall-clock budget, compute
budget, LLM budget, `no_improvement_rounds` rounds without improvement, crash
limit (repeated unfixable crashes), `max_rounds`, user stop. Before a budget
would be exceeded to finish valuable work (for example a seed check in flight),
the master files a `budget_extension` approval instead of overrunning.

### 3.8 Locks (`state/locks.py`)
`fcntl.flock` locks under `locks/`, each with a JSON `LockInfo` sidecar (holder
pid, host, owner, acquired time) for display:

- `master.lock`: held for the master's lifetime; a second master fails fast and
  names the holder.
- `run-<run_id>.lock`: held by the run supervisor; a run is never driven twice.
- `device-<device_id>.lock`: held by the run supervisor; two runs never share a
  device.

flock releases on process death, so a lock probe (non-blocking try, release at
once) is how recovery tells a live supervisor from a dead one. No PID guessing.

### 3.9 Steering inbox and status events (`state/inbox.py`)
Master to worker: one JSON `InboxMessage` file per message in
`workers/<id>/inbox/<seq>-<msg_id>.json`, written atomically (temp file and
rename), processed in sequence order, acknowledged by moving it to
`inbox/handled/`. After writing, the master nudges the pane with a short line
("autoexp: inbox has N messages") using `herdr pane send-text` and Enter.

Worker to master: `WorkerEvent` lines appended to `workers/<id>/events.jsonl`
(`idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `takeover`, `done`, with run ID and note). Run
supervisors append `RunEvent` lines to `runs/<run_id>/events.jsonl`.

### 3.10 Human takeover
Human input wins. The master types into a pane only when (a) the worker has no
`takeover` marker (`autoexp worker takeover <id> on|off`, also a dashboard
button) and (b) Herdr reports the pane's agent `idle`. A pane that is busy
without a master nudge is treated as human-driven and steering holds. Held
messages stay in the durable inbox and are delivered after release.

### 3.11 Herdr adapter (`herdr/`)
`HerdrAdapter` protocol: create workspace, split pane, run a command in a pane,
read pane output, send text and keys, get agent state. `CliHerdrAdapter` shells
out with a configurable command prefix, so a deployment can point it at a named
session (`herdr --session <name>`) or at a wrapper script. `FakeHerdr` backs
the tests.

### 3.12 Approvals (`state/approvals.py`)
`ApprovalRequest` files in `approvals/<approval_id>.json` (`code_change`,
`budget_extension`), answered by `autoexp approve|reject <id>` or the dashboard,
which writes `<approval_id>.decision.json`. Pending approvals never block the
loop; only the gated action waits.

### 3.13 Dashboard (`dashboard/`)
Standard-library HTTP server bound to `127.0.0.1`. It reads the state directory
(read-only except for approval answers, takeover toggles and the stop flag,
which require a same-origin JSON POST). Views: runs by run ID with status and
device, return curves, prune and decision events with their reasoning, budgets,
pending approvals, worker panes, and the final finding.

### 3.14 Keeping the user updated
Three channels from the same events: the dashboard, a one-line digest per
significant event in the master's terminal, and `autoexp status` for a text
summary.

## 4. Durable state layout

Everything is keyed by run ID (`r0001`, `r0002`, ...). Default root:
`./autoexp-state/<experiment_id>/` (git-ignored).

```text
experiment.json                 config snapshot + experiment id
counters.json                   next run id, next inbox sequence
STOP                            user stop flag (presence = stop)
finding.md                      final written finding
master/events.jsonl             decisions, prunes, budget, round, stop events
master/heartbeat.json           last tick time, pid
master/offsets.json             telemetry read offsets (cache, rebuildable)
locks/master.lock (+ .json)
locks/run-<run_id>.lock (+ .json)
locks/device-<device_id>.lock (+ .json)
runs/<run_id>/spec.json         RunSpec (immutable once written)
runs/<run_id>/events.jsonl      RunEvent lines (lifecycle)
runs/<run_id>/metrics.jsonl     TelemetryEvent lines (trainer)
runs/<run_id>/stdout.log        trainer stdout+stderr
runs/<run_id>/control.json      stop request from the worker to the supervisor
runs/<run_id>/checkpoints/
workers/<worker_id>/worker.json pane id, runtime, assigned devices
workers/<worker_id>/inbox/<seq>-<msg_id>.json
workers/<worker_id>/inbox/handled/
workers/<worker_id>/events.jsonl
workers/<worker_id>/takeover    human takeover marker
approvals/<approval_id>.json
approvals/<approval_id>.decision.json
```

## 5. Recovery

`recover(layout, locks) -> RecoveryReport` (`state/recovery.py`) runs at master
start before the first tick:

1. Take `master.lock` or exit.
2. Fold every `runs/*/events.jsonl` into `RunRecord`s.
3. For each non-terminal run, probe its run lock: held means the supervisor is
   alive and the run is re-adopted; free means it died and the run becomes
   `lost` (the decision engine may retry it under a new run ID).
4. Replay master intents whose effect is missing (an allocated run without its
   assign message, a prune verdict without its stop message).
5. Re-open missing worker panes for worker IDs that own live runs.
6. Rebuild telemetry offsets (a cache; rescanning from zero is always correct).

## 6. Configuration and machine defaults

One TOML file (`configs/cartpole.toml`) drives search space, pruning, budgets,
stop rules, workers, devices, Herdr and LLM settings (`config/schema.py`).
Defaults for this Mac (Apple M1, 8 cores, 16 GB, CPU only): 2 workers x 2 runs,
4 device slots `cpu0..cpu3` with 2 torch threads each, hard cap of 4 concurrent
training processes. An `mps` slot can be enabled, but a small PPO MLP is faster
on CPU.

## 7. Command surface (`cli.py`)

```text
autoexp up --config FILE            master + dashboard (single start command)
autoexp status                      text summary of runs, budgets, approvals
autoexp stop                        set the user stop flag
autoexp approve|reject ID           answer a pending approval
autoexp dashboard                   dashboard only, read state
autoexp worker handle --worker ID   process the inbox once (used by both runtimes)
autoexp worker serve --worker ID    ShellRuntime loop
autoexp worker report --worker ID   append a WorkerEvent
autoexp worker takeover ID on|off   human takeover marker
autoexp run-exec RUN_ID             run supervisor (spawned by the worker)
```

## 8. Testing strategy

Deterministic parts are tested without Herdr or an LLM: run ID allocation,
locks (two processes), registry folding, recovery against seeded state dirs,
each pruning rule on synthetic curves, stop rules on synthetic ledgers,
telemetry parsing with partial lines, decision validation. Herdr goes through
`FakeHerdr`, the LLM through a fake `LLMClient`. An end-to-end proof runs the
milestone in a real Herdr session with real CartPole training.

## 9. Out of scope for v1

Remote machines or clusters; W&B, TensorBoard or MLflow; environments other

Captain, the architecture is ready for your review: **http://127.0.0.1:4387/session/7c8d2352112f56f8**

It's committed on the worker's branch and not pushed. There are two parts:
- **An architecture document** with the diagram.
- **A typed Python code skeleton** of about 60 modules under `src/autoexp/`. The data models and interfaces are real code; the behaviour inside them is stubbed for now.

**How it's split:**
- **Plain code runs everything that controls the system:**
  - the master loop, scheduling and steering
  - the locks: one master, one driver per run, one run per device
  - the run registry and crash recovery
  - telemetry parsing
  - pruning by plateau, divergence and successive halving / ASHA
  - budgets and stop rules
  - approvals, and the dashboard
- **The AI model sits at only 3 points:**
  - proposing what to run next
  - an optional pruner that judges training curves
  - the coding agent inside each worker that debugs crashed runs

  Each of these has a plain-code fallback, and code checks every AI output before it takes effect.
- **Workers** are Herdr panes. A small supervisor process holds each run, so training keeps going even if a pane or its agent dies.
- **Everything is stored as files on disk, keyed by run ID**, and the master recovers it all after a crash.
- **Your input in a pane always wins.** A takeover switch and a busy-pane check stop the master typing over you.
- **Start and control:** one `autoexp up` command starts the master and the dashboard. `status`, `stop` and `approve`/`reject` work from the terminal.

**What I need from you:** on the page, select any text to comment on it, then choose **Approve**, **Approve with changes**, or **Revise**. The worker builds the full system once you approve. I'm waiting on your verdict, and the main first mate has the same link.

- **The frontend gets its own folder.** It has an `index.html` plus plain modern JavaScript modules, with no build step. It covers:

  - the prune and decision feed with the reasoning
  - budgets, plus approve and reject buttons for pending approvals

### 3.13 Dashboard (`dashboard/`): JavaScript frontend, Python JSON API

The dashboard is split into a browser frontend and a Python backend. They
share only the JSON contract in `dashboard/schemas.py`.

**Backend** (Python, standard library `ThreadingHTTPServer`, bound to
`127.0.0.1`):

- `server.py` serves the frontend's static files from `dashboard/web/`
  (`/` and `/static/...`, refusing any path outside that directory) and sends
  `/api/...` requests through `routes.py` to `handlers.py`.
- `handlers.py` reads the state directory through `views.py`, which are pure
  builders from files to DTOs. The backend never talks to Herdr or to workers.
  The master's observer caches each pane's tail in `workers/<id>/pane.txt`,
  and the dashboard reads that file.
- Only three writes are allowed: an approval decision file, a worker takeover
  marker, and the `STOP` flag. The master picks each one up on its next tick.
  Every POST needs `Content-Type: application/json` and an `Origin` that
  matches the server's own origin; bodies are capped at 4 KiB and validated.

Every response uses one envelope:
`{"ok": bool, "data": <shape> | null, "error": {"code", "message"} | null}`.

| Method | Path | Response `data` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/overview` | `OverviewDTO`: `experiment_id`, `goal` (metric, window, threshold, seeds_required), `version`, `round_index`, `master` (running/stopped/absent), `stop_requested`, `runs[]` (RunRowDTO), `workers[]`, `budget`, `approvals[]`, `finding` | what the page shows at a glance |
| GET | `/api/runs/{run_id}` | `RunDetailDTO`: `run`, `events[]` (lifecycle), `stdout_tail` | per-run drill-down |
| GET | `/api/runs/{run_id}/curve?since_step=N&max_points=M` | `CurveDTO`: `run_id`, `returns[{step, rolling_return, episode_return}]`, `losses[{step, policy_loss, value_loss, entropy, approx_kl}]`, `next_step` | incremental; `next_step` is the next `since_step` |
| GET | `/api/events?after=SEQ&kinds=prune,decision` | `EventsDTO`: `events[{seq, at, kind, summary, data}]`, `next_seq` | prune `data`: `run_id, pruner, reason, evidence`; decision `data`: `engine, action, rationale, fallback_reason, proposals` |
| GET | `/api/workers/{worker_id}/pane?lines=N` | `PaneDTO`: `worker_id`, `pane_id`, `text`, `read_at` | cached pane tail |
| GET | `/api/stream` | server-sent events | `event: version` with `{"version": N}`, keepalive comment every 15 s |
| POST | `/api/approvals/{approval_id}` | `ApprovalDTO` | body `{"decision": "approve"\|"reject", "note"}`; 409 if no longer pending |
| POST | `/api/workers/{worker_id}/takeover` | `WorkerDTO` | body `{"on": bool}` |
| POST | `/api/stop` | `OverviewDTO` | sets the user stop flag |

`RunRowDTO` holds `run_id, round_index, purpose, parent_run_id, status,
worker_id, device_id, seed, config, step, total_steps, rolling_return,
best_rolling_return, sps, stop_reason, started_at, ended_at`.

**Refresh.** `overview.version` is derived from the sizes and modification
times of the state files the overview depends on. `/api/stream` pushes a
`version` event whenever that value changes. The UI then refetches the
overview, any events after its `next_seq` cursor, incremental curves for the
runs on screen, and the pane tails. If the stream fails, the UI polls the
overview every 3 s and tries the stream again after 15 s.

**Frontend** (`dashboard/web/`, plain modern JavaScript ES modules, no build
step, no third-party code):

```text
web/index.html               layout, CSP (self only), loads js/main.js as a module
web/css/style.css
web/js/main.js               wires store + API + refresh + components
web/js/api.js                fetch client, envelope unwrapping, ApiError, JSDoc mirror of schemas.py
web/js/store.js              immutable store (frozen state, pure reducers, subscribe)
web/js/refresh.js            SSE with polling fallback
web/js/dom.js                h()/s() element builders; data is inserted as text, never as HTML
web/js/format.js             display formatting
web/js/charts/lineChart.js   dependency-free SVG line chart (multi-series, goal line)
web/js/components/runsTable.js   runs by run ID; click a row to select it for the curves
web/js/components/curves.js      rolling return (with the goal line), value loss, approx KL
web/js/components/feed.js        prune and decision feed with reasoning and fallback reason
web/js/components/budgets.js     budget lines with progress bars
web/js/components/approvals.js   pending approvals with approve / reject
web/js/components/workers.js     worker state, runs, pane tail, takeover toggle
web/js/components/controls.js    master state, stop button
web/js/components/finding.js     final finding when the loop has ended
```

Why there is no build step and no charting library: the UI is a handful of
panels and line charts. A small SVG chart module avoids vendoring third-party
code into a public repository and keeps the frontend runnable straight from
the Python package. If the charts outgrow it, `charts/lineChart.js` is the only
module that would change. The pure frontend modules (`store.js`, and later the
formatting and chart scaling) are unit-tested with `node --test`, which needs
no dependencies.

### 3.14 Keeping the user updated

### 3.13 Dashboard (`dashboard/`): JavaScript frontend, Python JSON API

The dashboard is split into a browser frontend and a Python backend. They
share only the JSON contract in `dashboard/schemas.py`.

**Backend** (Python, standard library `ThreadingHTTPServer`, bound to
`127.0.0.1`):

- `server.py` serves the frontend's static files from `dashboard/web/`
  (`/` and `/static/...`, refusing any path outside that directory) and sends
  `/api/...` requests through `routes.py` to `handlers.py`.
- `handlers.py` reads the state directory through `views.py`, which are pure
  builders from files to DTOs. The backend never talks to Herdr or to workers.
  The master's observer caches each pane's tail in `workers/<id>/pane.txt`,
  and the dashboard reads that file.
- Only three writes are allowed: an approval decision file, a worker takeover
  marker, and the `STOP` flag. The master picks each one up on its next tick.
  Every POST needs `Content-Type: application/json` and an `Origin` that
  matches the server's own origin; bodies are capped at 4 KiB and validated.

Every response uses one envelope:
`{"ok": bool, "data": <shape> | null, "error": {"code", "message"} | null}`.

| Method | Path | Response `data` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/overview` | `OverviewDTO`: `experiment_id`, `goal` (metric, window, threshold, seeds_required), `version`, `round_index`, `master` (running/stopped/absent), `stop_requested`, `runs[]` (RunRowDTO), `workers[]`, `budget`, `approvals[]`, `finding` | what the page shows at a glance |
| GET | `/api/runs/{run_id}` | `RunDetailDTO`: `run`, `events[]` (lifecycle), `stdout_tail` | per-run drill-down |
| GET | `/api/runs/{run_id}/curve?since_step=N&max_points=M` | `CurveDTO`: `run_id`, `returns[{step, rolling_return, episode_return}]`, `losses[{step, policy_loss, value_loss, entropy, approx_kl}]`, `next_step` | incremental; `next_step` is the next `since_step` |
| GET | `/api/events?after=SEQ&kinds=prune,decision` | `EventsDTO`: `events[{seq, at, kind, summary, data}]`, `next_seq` | prune `data`: `run_id, pruner, reason, evidence`; decision `data`: `engine, action, rationale, fallback_reason, proposals` |
| GET | `/api/workers/{worker_id}/pane?lines=N` | `PaneDTO`: `worker_id`, `pane_id`, `text`, `read_at` | cached pane tail |
| GET | `/api/stream` | server-sent events | `event: version` with `{"version": N}`, keepalive comment every 15 s |
| POST | `/api/approvals/{approval_id}` | `ApprovalDTO` | body `{"decision": "approve"\|"reject", "note"}`; 409 if no longer pending |
| POST | `/api/workers/{worker_id}/takeover` | `WorkerDTO` | body `{"on": bool}` |
| POST | `/api/stop` | `OverviewDTO` | sets the user stop flag |

`RunRowDTO` holds `run_id, round_index, purpose, parent_run_id, status,
worker_id, device_id, seed, config, step, total_steps, rolling_return,
best_rolling_return, sps, stop_reason, started_at, ended_at`.

**Refresh.** `overview.version` is derived from the sizes and modification
times of the state files the overview depends on. `/api/stream` pushes a
`version` event whenever that value changes. The UI then refetches the
overview, any events after its `next_seq` cursor, incremental curves for the
runs on screen, and the pane tails. If the stream fails, the UI polls the
overview every 3 s and tries the stream again after 15 s.

**Frontend** (`dashboard/web/`, plain modern JavaScript ES modules, no build
step, no third-party code):

```text
web/index.html               layout, CSP (self only), loads js/main.js as a module
web/css/style.css
web/js/main.js               wires store + API + refresh + components
web/js/api.js                fetch client, envelope unwrapping, ApiError, JSDoc mirror of schemas.py
web/js/store.js              immutable store (frozen state, pure reducers, subscribe)
web/js/refresh.js            SSE with polling fallback
web/js/dom.js                h()/s() element builders; data is inserted as text, never as HTML
web/js/format.js             display formatting
web/js/charts/lineChart.js   dependency-free SVG line chart (multi-series, goal line)

web/js/components/workers.js     worker state, runs, pane tail, takeover toggle
web/js/components/controls.js    master state, stop button
web/js/components/finding.js     final finding when the loop has ended
```

Captain, the revised architecture is on the same review page: **http://127.0.0.1:4387/session/7c8d2352112f56f8**. Reload it if it's already open.

**What changed:** the dashboard is now a real HTML and JavaScript frontend (section 3.13). It lives in `dashboard/web/`:
- **The page:** `index.html` and a stylesheet.
- **Plain JavaScript modules** with no build step and no third-party code:
  - an API client
  - a state store
  - live refresh: the page updates the moment anything changes, and falls back to checking every 3 seconds if that stream drops
  - a small charting module written for this project
- **Nine panels:**
  - the runs table by run ID
  - return and loss curves with the goal line
  - the prune and decision feed with the reasoning
  - budget bars
  - approve and reject buttons for pending approvals
  - worker panes with a takeover switch
  - the stop button, master status, and the final finding
- **The backend** is a Python JSON API with 9 documented endpoints. It only reads the run data, except for three allowed writes: answering approvals, the takeover switch, and the stop flag.

The rest of the architecture is unchanged, and nothing is pushed yet. Choose **Approve**, **Approve with changes**, or **Revise** on the page. The worker builds the full system once you approve.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: ~/.treehouse/firstmate-7bab20/2/firstmate/.claude/skills/validation-supervision

# Validation supervision

For a no-mistakes ship, trigger validation on the same worker after its implementation commit, using the harness invocation owned by `harness-adapters`.
The task worker that starts a no-mistakes run drives the pipeline and owns every `no-mistakes axi run` and `no-mistakes axi respond` call through the next gate or outcome.
Firstmate never invokes `no-mistakes axi respond` for a crew-owned run.
`bin/fm-dod-lib.sh` owns the worker-side `--intent` contract.
Once validation starts, prefer routing new requirements to follow-up work rather than expanding the current task, unless a new requirement completely invalidates the work being validated; however, the smallest downstream changes needed to keep already accepted product or engineering behavior correct, add behavioral tests where an executable contract exists, or keep documentation accurate remain within the current task even when they touch files not named at intake, and corrections required to satisfy already accepted intent are not new requirements.

Only a current, explicit captain instruction that completely invalidates the work being validated keeps the task with the same worker instead of routing it to follow-up work or handing it to a replacement.
That worker cancels the active run through no-mistakes axi's supported abort command and confirms through axi status that the run has stopped before changing any code.
The worker then follows `branch_sync.next_action` from structured axi status: use axi sync's supported guarded recovery only when its code is `recover_custody`, and otherwise proceed only when structured status confirms that branch ownership is already returned and no recovery is required.
Custody recovery settles branch ownership, not content: the worker must replace the obsolete work from the correct pre-invalidation base rather than building on top of the recovered-but-obsolete head, keeping the obsolete run's own pipeline-fix commits out of what gets validated and shipped.
Apart from that single supported abort, do not hand-edit, commit, restart, or start a second validation run while the obsolete run still owns the branch.
Once ownership is settled, validate exactly once against that final head so no obsolete or intermediate head is ever treated as authoritative.

An ask-user finding returns as `needs-decision`; firstmate loads `ask-user-authority` and either decides or escalates per that skill.
Send the same worker one exact decision naming the decision key, step, action, affected finding IDs, instructions where needed, and exact response command, passing `--resolve-key` so the worker's open decision record closes at answer time.
Require the matching `resolved` event, forbid `--yes`, and require the worker to process every synchronous return until completion or a genuinely new escalation.
Resume fleet supervision immediately after the decision lands.

Judge validation by the resolved state line from [`bin/fm-crew-state.sh`](../../../bin/fm-crew-state.sh), whose header owns outcome mappings and CI-monitor/daemon exceptions, never by shell liveness, the last status event, or a raw run record.
Workers parked at approval or fix-review must follow the active gate help.
A worker hand-editing, committing, aborting, or restarting during an active validation run duplicates pipeline ownership outside the supersession sequence above; steer it back to the gate response flow.
The worker reports the PR when CI first becomes green rather than waiting for merge monitoring to finish.

Captain, the full build is finished and is going through validation now.

**What was built** (it matches the approved architecture):
- the master/worker loop, with locks, crash recovery, pruning, and decisions made by the AI with a plain-code fallback
- the HTML + JavaScript dashboard on top of the Python JSON API
- 122 Python tests and 8 JavaScript tests

**The proof run** happened in an isolated Herdr session:
- The master ran the 4 CartPole configs and found a winner that held up on 3 seeds.
- Taking over a pane, typing into a worker's pane, and recovering after the master was killed outright all worked.

**Next:** the work is going through the full validation pipeline, with the CI step skipped because the repo has none. That ends in a pull request carrying the proof summary, a dashboard screenshot, and the defaults list (training code, worker model, concurrency, stop rules, AI tool, MIT license) so you can overrule any of them. If the review raises anything only you can decide, I'll bring it to you. Otherwise the next thing you'll get is the pull request link, and the merge stays yours.

1. **Push the cleaned branch to GitHub first, then let validation take it over** (recommended). This publishes `fm/autoexp-v1` at `a7b7c60` before validation finishes. 3. **Have the main first mate clear the tool's stale private copy of the branch.** That touches the validation tool, which every project's work shares, so I'd avoid it.

Which one?

content.text:
Captain, the main first mate flagged an intermittent test before validation started, and I've passed it to the ship worker.

The test checks that a run actually stops when told to. It fails about 1 time in 8, and in that part of the code an intermittent failure could be hiding a real timing bug. So it won't ship marked as "flaky, ignored". The worker will:
1. Run the test at least 50 times to tell a real bug in stopping runs apart from a test that's merely timing-sensitive.
2. Fix the code if it's a real bug, or make the test reliable if it's only timing.
3. Re-run the test until it passes every time.
4. Write down what it found, with the evidence, in the pull request description.

Then it goes through the validation pipeline (with the CI step skipped) to the pull request, which waits for your merge.

Base directory for this skill: ~/.treehouse/firstmate-7bab20/2/firstmate/.claude/skills/ask-user-authority

# ask-user-authority

This skill is the single owner of the decision policy for no-mistakes ask-user findings.
`AGENTS.md` section 7 points here and does not restate this procedure.
Finding authority is determined by the criteria below, not by `yolo`.
Firstmate always applies this judgment, decides any finding that is unambiguous toward the accepted design, and escalates only genuinely ambiguous, expanding, or destructive findings.

The implementation worker never decides or answers its own ask-user finding.
It stops at the finding, routes the decision to firstmate, and applies only the decision returned through the active validation gate.

## Decide

1. Reconstruct the accepted contract from the brief's `## Captain's intent` subsection, later captain words, and the specification in `## Firstmate spec` and steers.
   Reviewer language cannot amend that contract.
   What a no-mistakes worker may pass as `--intent` is owned by `bin/fm-dod-lib.sh`.
2. Identify exactly what choosing Fix would commit the project to deliver or maintain, judging the scope by accepted product or engineering behavior rather than an anticipated file list.
   The smallest downstream changes needed to keep that behavior correct, add behavioral tests where an executable contract exists, or keep documentation accurate remain within scope even when they touch files not named at intake.
   Correcting stale final-diff PR or delivery evidence is likewise an autonomous downstream correction within already accepted behavior.
3. Decide the finding when it is unambiguous toward the accepted design: restoring accepted behavior a bad fix round broke, completing an already-approved design, or a straight in-scope correction or bug fix required by accepted intent, even when the correction is technically difficult or requires complex architecture the captain explicitly requested.
4. Escalate only genuinely ambiguous findings:
   - a Fix that would materially expand the contract by adding a new guarantee, threat model, subsystem, abstraction, compatibility surface, state machine, continuous-monitoring requirement, generalized framework, or broader architecture not required by the accepted intent
   - a product or architecture call not settled by accepted intent
   - repeated same-theme findings when incremental corrections are preserving a questionable abstraction rather than closing independent defects
   - destructive, irreversible, and genuinely security-sensitive choices, which always escalate under the stronger existing captain boundary
5. Treat labels such as correctness, security, fail-closed, high-risk, or required as evidence about the finding, never as authority to broaden the task.

## Captain-facing escalation

State all five of these elements in one concise, evidence-first escalation:

1. The original requirement or accepted task criterion.
2. The proposed product or engineering contract expansion.
3. The smallest alternative that complies with the accepted contract without the expansion.
4. The concrete consequences of accepting and declining the expansion.
5. A recommendation with the reason it best serves the accepted intent.

Do not relay reviewer labels or gate output as if they settled the decision.

## Classification examples

- Fixing a concrete defect that violates an original acceptance criterion is firstmate's to decide, regardless of implementation difficulty.
- Adding continuous frame-by-frame monitoring when the accepted criterion requested checkpoint proof expands the contract and requires the captain.
- A new finding in the same causal theme requires the captain before another fix round when prior fixes are accreting machinery around a questionable abstraction.
- A genuinely security-sensitive action requires the captain under the stronger existing boundary even if it is otherwise within scope.
- Complex architecture explicitly requested by the captain stays within scope and does not escalate merely because it is complex.

id: asha-pruned-rung-excluded
severity: info
file: src/autoexp/pruning/halving.py
line: 93
description: This is in code changed by the Round 1 fix 'asha-pool-excludes-pruned', and that fix only partly closes the gap. A PRUNED run now counts as a peer only at rungs found in decided_rungs. decided_rungs (seen_rungs) records only halving KEEP verdicts (phases.py:287-293, loop.py:80-83). So a run is still left out at the rung where it was pruned, even though it legitimately reported a value there. Standard ASHA, and the Round 1 finding itself, would only exclude rungs after the pruning rung. Example (async, eta=2, rung 1): A=100 and B=50 report, and B is pruned at rung 1. Later C=70 and D=60 reach rung 1. The pool is {A,C,D} with keep=1, so C is pruned. With B in the pool, keep=2 and C would continue. The smallest remedy means tracking each pruned run's pruning rung. Today seen_prunes holds only run ids, so that is new loop state, which is why this is ask-user. Sync mode, the default, is unaffected.

The review flagged one bug in pruning. In ASHA mode, a run pruned at a checkpoint stopped counting as a comparison point at that same checkpoint. As a result, a later run could be cut that standard ASHA would keep. The default pruning mode isn't affected. ASHA is part of your accepted requirements, so I decided this one myself and told the worker to fix it. The fix records the checkpoint where each pruned run was cut, saves it to disk so it survives a restart, and adds a test that reproduces the reviewer's example.

The pipeline continues to the pull request, which waits for your merge.

<pasted_content id="75a1">
# Task: Write My AI-Assisted Project Reflection for the Take-Home Exercise

## Context

I am completing a take-home exercise for an AI research/engineering opportunity. The evaluators are interested in **how I work with AI, how I steer it, how I make technical decisions, and how I critically evaluate its outputs**. They are not simply evaluating the complexity of the final project.

The submission requires:
1. The final project artefact.
2. Raw, unedited AI–human interaction transcripts.
3. A short reflection addressing:
   - What I did
   - Clarity of the project
   - How I steered the AI
   - Where AI helped and where it got in the way
   - Results and learnings

Your task is to write the third component.

**Do not start writing immediately. First reconstruct what actually happened using our conversation history, available project documentation, specifications, commits, and code.**

## Project Overview

I built a system combining:

- **Observability:** Herdr, providing visibility into experiments, execution, metrics, and research workflows.
- **Autonomous Research:** An autoresearch-inspired framework for generating, executing, evaluating, and iterating on ML experiments.
- **ML Intern:** A Hugging Face-oriented ML experimentation workflow involving training, hyperparameter exploration, and experiment evaluation.
- **Agent Orchestration:** FirstMate and the Claude Code harness, with components responsible for research-level decisions and experiment execution.

The project integrates ideas and code from four repositories: Herdr, FirstMate, autoresearch, and ML Intern.

Verify the actual responsibilities of these components from the code. Do not assume my high-level descriptions are perfectly accurate.

## How I Worked With AI

### Phase 1: Interactive Product Specification

I began with interactive, UI-driven product specification and clarification using the Lavish editor.

Instead of giving Claude a single vague prompt to implement the entire application, I worked on defining the system requirements first.

We explored and clarified:
- The responsibilities and boundaries of the different components.
- How the four repositories should work together.
- A master–worker (or master–slave) orchestration architecture.
- How an agent should reason about experiments versus simply executing them.
- Parallel experiments, concurrency, resource constraints, and locking.
- Experiment tracking and observability.
- Evaluation metrics, stopping criteria, and experiment selection.
- Hyperparameter optimization and early-stopping methods, including ASHA.
- The interfaces and contracts between components.

Identify additional important decisions from the actual specifications and conversations.

### Phase 2: Architecture Exploration and Design Iteration

I did not accept the first architecture Claude proposed.

I actively reviewed the design, questioned assumptions, evaluated trade-offs, and iterated on the architecture **twice before arriving at the design I wanted**.

Describe the actual architectural alternatives, feedback, changes, and reasoning where these are documented.

Make clear that Claude was a collaborator in the design process, but that I was responsible for defining objectives, reviewing proposals, identifying weaknesses, and deciding what to adopt.

### Phase 3: Independent Research and Verification

I used Claude for design discussions, but also performed my own research through web searches and ChatGPT.

I explored concepts such as:
- Experiment scheduling and resource allocation.
- ASHA and efficient hyperparameter optimization.
- Choosing meaningful evaluation metrics.
- Stopping experiments and determining whether an experiment is promising.
- Agent autonomy versus deterministic execution.
- Concurrency, locking, and orchestration design.
- Observability for ML research workflows.

Explain how independent research informed my decisions and how I brought those insights back into Claude discussions.

Where possible, identify moments when I challenged or corrected an AI suggestion based on my own reasoning or external research.

### Phase 4: Implementation and Verification

Using Claude Code with the Herdr and FirstMate tooling, I moved from the agreed specification to implementation.

Inspect the repository, code changes, execution logs, tests, and conversations to determine:
- What was actually implemented.
- Which parts of the system were adapted or integrated from existing repositories.
- What Claude generated or modified.
- What I reviewed, corrected, or explicitly directed.
- How the implementation was checked against the specification.
- Which tests or experiments were actually run.
- Which features remain incomplete or unverified.

Do not confuse planned capabilities with implemented or tested results.

## What I Want the Reflection to Demonstrate

The most important theme is:

**I used AI to accelerate engineering and research, but I did not delegate the thinking, decision-making, or evaluation entirely to it.**

Show evidence of the following, without making these sound like generic claims:

1. **Problem formulation:** I transformed an ambitious idea into a concrete, testable specification.
2. **Technical judgment:** I made decisions about architecture, evaluation, experiment scheduling, and system constraints.
3. **Iterative steering:** I challenged AI-generated proposals and refined the design through multiple iterations.
4. **Research mindset:** I independently investigated unfamiliar concepts rather than accepting Claude's suggestions unquestioningly.
5. **Verification:** I checked the design and implementation against requirements.
6. **Effective use of AI:** I used AI where it was useful, while retaining ownership of important technical decisions.
7. **Critical reflection:** I can articulate specific limitations, mistakes, friction, and trade-offs encountered while working with AI.

## Important: Discuss Where AI Got in the Way

Do not make this a promotional write-up for Claude.

Investigate the transcript for real examples of:
- Incorrect architectural assumptions.
- Overly complicated designs.
- Incomplete understanding of requirements.
- Suggestions that conflicted with constraints.
- Repeated clarification or context loss.
- Implementation that diverged from the specification.
- Areas requiring human intervention or independent research.

Include only examples supported by evidence.

A credible discussion of what did not work is more valuable than claiming the entire experience was seamless.

## Output Requirements

Write the final reflection under these headings:

### 1. What I Built
Briefly explain the integrated system and its purpose.

### 2. Project Clarity and Specification
Explain how I clarified the problem, defined component responsibilities, and established constraints before implementation.

### 3. How I Steered the AI
Describe my interaction with Claude, the design iterations, independent research, architectural decisions, and verification.

### 4. Where AI Helped and Where It Got in the Way
Give concrete examples of both strengths and limitations.

### 5. Results and Key Learnings
Summarize what was implemented, demonstrated, tested, and learned.

## Writing Style

- Write in **first person** ("I").
- Use natural, technically precise language.
- Sound like a thoughtful ML research engineer reflecting on an actual project.
- Keep it concise: approximately **350–450 words**.
- Bullet points are acceptable, but avoid making every sentence a bullet.
- Avoid corporate language and exaggerated claims.
- Do not make this sound like an AI-generated cover letter.
- Do not claim I built all four underlying projects from scratch.
- Preserve technical details such as ASHA, experiment orchestration, stopping criteria, observability, and locking when relevant.
- Do not invent benchmarks, performance improvements, successful experiments, or capabilities.
- Focus more on **my decisions and my interactions with AI** than on listing features.

## Required Process

**Step 1:** Inspect relevant conversation history, specifications, design documents, repository changes, and evaluation results.

**Step 2:** Reconstruct the project's chronology, including the initial requirements, two major design iterations, final architecture, and implementation.

**Step 3:** Identify five to eight concrete examples of human steering, AI assistance, or AI limitations, with evidence from the actual work.

**Step 4:** Distinguish verified facts from information that is only described in the prompt.

**Step 5:** Write the final polished reflection using the requested five headings.

**Step 6:** Perform a final accuracy check against the available project evidence.

If any significant claims cannot be verified, either qualify or omit them.

**Final objective:** The reader should understand not just what I built, but how I used AI to formulate the problem, explore designs, challenge assumptions, make decisions, and produce and evaluate a technical artefact. The reflection should communicate intellectual ownership, curiosity, and engineering judgment without overstating my contribution or the system's capabilities.

Output the final reflection first. Then provide a short section titled "Evidence worth including" identifying the most convincing conversation excerpts, design revisions, or test results that I should point reviewers toward. Do not modify or tidy the raw transcripts.
</pasted_content id="75a1">

## Proof: the milestone, run for real in a Herdr lab session

All three runs used real CartPole PPO training (`trainers/ppo_cartpole.py`, CPU), two Claude Code worker panes (`--model sonnet`) in an isolated Herdr session, and the **LLM decision engine** (`claude -p --output-format json --model sonnet`) with its deterministic fallback armed. The deterministic e

![Milestone dashboard](docs/images/milestone-dashboard.png)

**Run 1: milestone config as committed (`configs/cartpole.toml`), 72 s, stopped by `goal_reached`**

| run | round | purpose | seed | status | best rolling return (100 ep) | config |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| r0001 | 1 | explore | 1 | pruned (halving, rung 0) | 404.5 | lr 2.5e-4, envs 4, steps 128, ent 0.01, clip 0.2, epochs 4 |
| r0002 | 1 | explore | 1 | pruned (halving, rung 0) | 463.3 | lr 1e-3, ent 0, clip 0.2, epochs 4 |
| r0003 | 1 | explore | 1 | pruned (halving, rung 0) | 389.8 | lr 2.5e-4, envs 8, steps 256, clip 0.1, epochs 10 |
| r0004 | 1 | explore | 1 | **solved** | 493.4 | lr 3e-3, ent 0.02, clip 0.3, epochs 2 |
| r0005 | 2 | seed_check | 2 | **solved** | 494.4 | same as r0004 |
| r0006 | 2 | seed_check | 3 | **solved** | 485.7 | same as r0004 |

The winner (lr 3e-3, clip 0.3, ent 0.02, 2 epochs, 4x128 rollouts) held mean return >= 475 over 100 episodes on seeds 1, 2 and 3. The finding (shown on the dashboard) includes the decision agent's explanation. The master typed nudges into both worker panes and held them while an agent was busy (`ste

**Run 2: same milestone with 100k-step runs and 1 thread per slot, so nothing solves early, 4 rounds, stopped by `max_rounds`**
- Two LLM exploration rounds with per-proposal reasoning, for example "Slightly lower lr and ent_coef than r0004 to improve stability ...".
- The verification protocol refuted a candidate: r0006 solved on seed 1 and r0010 on seed 3, but the seed-2 check r0009 peaked at 442.7, so exploration resumed.
- Human takeover of w2 through the dashboard: the master logged `holding messages for w2: human takeover` and assigned no new runs to w2 until it was released.
- `autoexp pane send w1 ...`: the master typed a status check into the idle Claude Code pane.
- The master was SIGKILLed after round 4 started and restarted from disk (`master started ... (resumed)`). It recorded the runs that ended while it was down and stopped by its rules.

**Run 3: recovery, SIGKILL during round 1**
- Killed while r0001, r0002 and r0003 were training. 10 s later r0002 was still training on its own (its supervisor holds the run and device locks).
- The restarted master logged `recovered: adopted ['r0002'], lost [], replayed []`. It picked up the outcomes of the runs that finished during the outage, verified r0002's config on seeds 2 and 3, and stopped on `goal_reached`.

Budgets at the end of run 2: wall clock 115 s / 1800, 1.34M env steps / 6M, 3 LLM calls / 20, $0.43 / $2.00. In run 1 the screenshot's LLM line reads 0 because the narrative call happened after the last budget write. That was a bug found in this proof and fixed in `15b881c`; run 2 shows the correcte

Bugs the lab runs surfaced, all fixed with tests:
- halving re-judged a run at a rung it had already passed;
- the finding text missed runs that reached the goal without a verified winner;
- the final budget missed the narrative call;
- approved code changes were never delivered to a worker;
- chart layout and axis ticks were wrong.

## Defaults chosen (the captain can revisit any of these)
- **License:** MIT, a default choice the captain can change.
- **Worker model:** the master is the only decider. Each worker is a Claude Code agent in its own Herdr pane (`--model sonnet`). It runs the configs assigned to it (2 per pane, through detached run supervisors), debugs crashes on request and reports `retry`/`unfixable`, and never chooses what to run
- **Concurrency:** 2 worker panes x 2 runs = the 4 CartPole configs, a hard cap of 4 concurrent training processes, device slots `cpu0..cpu3` with 2 torch threads each (CPU beats MPS for this small MLP).
- **Training code:** CleanRL-style single-file PPO on Gymnasium CartPole-v1, CPU only, 300k steps per run. Any program that writes the run's telemetry JSONL can be a trainer.
- **Goal:** mean return >= 475 over the last 100 episodes, held on 3 seeds before a config is called the winner. Configs are explored on seed 1; seeds 2 and 3 only verify.
- **Stop rules, all in config:** user stop, goal reached, wall clock 3600 s, compute 14400 device-seconds, 6M env steps, LLM budget (20 calls / $2), 3 unfixable crashes, 3 rounds without improvement, 6 rounds.
- **Pruning:** divergence (NaN/inf, KL > 0.5 for 3 updates, value loss > 1e4), plateau (gain < 5 over 60k steps after 60k), synchronous successive halving (rungs at 25% and 50%, eta 2; ASHA is `mode = "async"`), LLM judge available but off.
- **Rounds are synchronous:** the next decision waits until the current round has ended.
- **Master runtime:** a Python control loop. LLM reasoning runs through Claude Code headless (`claude -p`, sonnet). Both the worker and decision commands are configurable.
- **Approvals:** training-code changes (from the LLM decision) and budget extensions (asked at 85% of a time budget while a winner is being verified) become pending approvals on the dashboard. An approved code change is delivered to worker w1's agent.
- **Worker agent spending is not metered** in v1; only the master's own LLM calls count against the LLM budget.
test: make supervisor stop-on-control test deterministic

The test wrote the stop request on a 1 s wall-clock timer while the fake
trainer finished its 3000-step budget in about 1.2 s and the supervisor polls
control.json once per second. When the stop landed just after a poll, the
trainer completed its full budget before the next poll, so the supervisor
correctly recorded 'completed' (no stop_requested event, exit 0, step 3000).
That is test timing, not a stop-path race: in 50 baseline runs all 9
failures had that shape and every pruned run had a stop_requested event.

The fake trainer gains an until_stopped option that ignores the step budget
(with a 60 s safety cap), the test writes the stop only after the trainer has
written metrics, and it asserts the stop_requested event and pruned exit
rather than a time window. 50 repeated runs: 9 failures before, 0 after.

Captain, here's the reflection, written from what this session's records, the repo and the worker's evidence actually show. The pull request hasn't opened yet: the final validation fix round is still running. The text reflects that, so update the last paragraph if you submit after the PR opens.

### 1. What I Built

`auto_experiment` is a master–worker system for running RL experiments on one machine. A deterministic Python master watches training telemetry, prunes weak runs, decides what to run next, and reports to a local dashboard. Workers are Claude Code agents in Herdr terminal panes. They execute what the master assigns and never choose what to run. Firstmate was the harness I built it with. I took its supervision pattern as a model (exclusive lock, durable inboxes, status events, human takeover), not its code. Karpathy's autoresearch and Hugging Face's ML Intern were inspiration for the idea, not code I integrated.

### 2. Project Clarity and Specification

I turned down a "thin working slice" and specified the system first on a Lavish review board. Each requirement was accepted, rejected or changed, and open questions were answered. The key correction was mine: separate deciding from executing. The master is the brain, and one pane can run several configs. Constraints I set:
- runs on this M1 only, with 2 concurrent workers
- JSONL telemetry
- pruning by successive halving/ASHA, plateau/divergence rules and LLM judgement, all driven by config and budget
- the master launches, prunes and forks on its own, but asks before code changes or budget overruns
- run IDs, locks and crash recovery
- first milestone: 4 CartPole configurations

### 3. How I Steered the AI

I asked for the architecture before any implementation, and "as code, not just prompts": typed interfaces and data models, with the LLM confined to three validated seams that each have a deterministic fallback. I rejected the first revision because its dashboard was a 13-line placeholder. The second revision made the frontend real HTML/JavaScript over a JSON API, and I approved it. I also caught a review diagram that rendered blank. When the validation tool deadlocked, I made the call to publish the cleaned branch, and then to ship on a fresh branch.

### 4. Where AI Helped and Where It Got in the Way

It helped with breadth. It produced an approximately 60-module skeleton fast, ran real proof runs, and its review caught a real ASHA bug: pruned runs were left out of the peer pool at the rung where they were pruned. It got in the way too:
- It committed a coverage file holding local paths to a public repo's branch history. Cleaning that up stalled the validation tool, cost a fresh branch, and left a stale branch on GitHub.
- It initially treated a stop-path test failure as "flaky". Fifty runs showed it was test timing, not a race, but only because that was demanded.
- Some intermediate turns blocked on approval rules for the very first commit.

### 5. Results and Key Learnings

Built and proven in a real Herdr session:
- 4 CartPole PPO configurations, with halving pruning
- an LLM decision round, and a winner verified on 3 seeds
- human takeover, and recovery after the master was killed

There are 118 passing Python tests and 8 JavaScript tests. Not yet verified: async ASHA in a live run, the LLM-judge pruner (off by default), and metering of worker-agent spending. My main lesson is that AI made breadth cheap, so my time went into specification, review and refusing plausible but wrong defaults.

---

### Evidence worth including

- **Requirements:** the two Lavish board rounds, especially your change to R-02 ("the agent remains the brain… deciding vs. executing") and your "you give me options" answer.
- **Your steering lines:** "architecture doc first", "as a code and stuff not just prompts", "where is dashboard ui must be js and html… must be java script", "not able to see components diagram", "Fresh branch name".
- **The pull request's proof section:** the run 1 table (winner held 475+ on seeds 1–3), the run 2 seed check refuting a candidate, and the run 3 `recovered: adopted ['r0002']` line.
- **Commit `7878460`:** 9 failures in 50 runs before, 0 after, with the timing-versus-race reasoning.
- **The ASHA finding and its fix,** plus the coverage-file and validation-deadlock episode as honest friction.

**Claims I couldn't verify, so I qualified or left them out:**
- **Code from four repos:** none of the four was integrated as code. Herdr is driven through its command-line tool. The `auto_experiment` project depends only on torch, gymnasium and numpy.
- **Herdr as metrics observability:** it isn't. Observability comes from the JSONL telemetry and the dashboard.
- **Web/ChatGPT research:** this session doesn't show it, so I didn't name specific instances. Add them yourself if you have records.
- **Some steering calls were made by the first mates, not you:**
  - deciding to strip the coverage file
  - the ASHA fix
  - making the stop test deterministic, which the main first mate required

  Those are attributed to the AI side or left neutral.

# auto_experiment: evidence of how I worked with AI

Project: `chaitu0032/auto_experiment`, a master–worker system for running RL experiments. A deterministic Python master observes training telemetry, prunes weak runs, decides the next round and reports to a local dashboard. Workers are Claude Code agents in Herdr panes.

## The AI tools I used and how they fit together

| Tool | What it is | How I used it |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Anthropic's agentic coding CLI | Every agent below is a Claude Code session. I talked to it in plain language in my terminal. |
| **Firstmate** | An open-source supervisor layer for Claude Code | My main session acted as the "first mate": it never edits project code itself. It writes instructions, launches worker agents in isolated git worktrees, watches them, and relays decisions to me. |
| **Second mate** | A persistent Firstmate home with its own charter | I gave auto_experiment its own second mate, so this project's work and records stayed separate from my other work. |
| **Herdr** | A terminal workspace manager for agents | Each worker agent ran in its own visible Herdr tab, so I could watch it or type into it (screenshots 07 and 09). The product I built also uses Herdr panes for its experiment workers. |
| **Lavish editor** | A local review surface for agent-made HTML | I used it to specify requirements and to review the architecture. I accepted, rejected or changed items, wrote comments, and sent structured answers back to the agent (screenshots 01–06). |
| **no-mistakes** | An automated validation pipeline | It reviews, tests, lint-checks and opens the pull request. Its review found real bugs, for example the ASHA pruning-pool gap (screenshots 08 and 09). |

## The workflow, step by step

1. **Asked for requirements, not code.** The first plan was a "thin working slice". I stopped it and asked for the requirements as a Lavish board instead (transcript 02, start).
2. **Requirements round 1, on the Lavish board.**
   - 13 requirements drawn from my own words, plus open questions (screenshot 01).
   - I changed R-02: the master is the brain that decides what to run; workers only execute, and one pane may run several configs (screenshots 02–03).
3. **Requirements round 2.** The agent pointed out a conflict between two of my answers, offered options for the success criteria, and proposed defaults. I said "just build it" on those defaults.
4. **Architecture first, as code.** I asked for the architecture before any implementation, and "as a code and stuff not just prompts". The result was a design document plus a typed Python skeleton, where an LLM may act only behind three validated seams, each with a deterministic fallback (screenshot 06).
5. **Rejected revision 1.** Its dashboard was a 13-line placeholder, and I required a real HTML + JavaScript UI. Revision 2 split the dashboard into a JavaScript frontend and a Python JSON API, and I approved it (screenshot 05). I also caught a component diagram that rendered blank, and it was redrawn.
6. **Implementation and proof.** A worker agent built the system and ran the milestone for real in an isolated Herdr session (screenshot 07):
   - 4 CartPole PPO configurations, with pruning and an LLM decision round
   - a winner verified on 3 seeds
   - human takeover, and recovery after the master was killed outright
7. **Validation.** The no-mistakes review found and fixed issues (screenshot 08). Problems along the way, which I decided how to handle:
   - A committed coverage file with local paths had to be removed from history.
   - The validation tool then deadlocked, and I chose to ship on a fresh branch.
   - An intermittent stop-path test had to be proven to be test timing rather than a race (50-run evidence).
   - The ASHA finding was fixed (screenshot 09).

## Contents

- `screenshots/`: evidence screenshots 01–09 in chronological order. Run `./copy-screenshots.sh` once to fill this folder from the Desktop.
- `transcripts/`: raw, unedited Claude Code session logs (`.jsonl`, one JSON object per line, exactly as Claude Code stored them):
  - `01-main-firstmate-session.jsonl`: my main session with the first mate
  - `02-secondmate-autoexp-session.jsonl`: the auto_experiment second mate (requirements, architecture review, decisions)
  - `03-worker-build-autoexp-v1.jsonl`: the worker that designed, built and proved the system
  - `04-worker-ship-autoexp-ship.jsonl`: the worker that shipped it on the fresh branch and ran validation
  - `05-worker-v1-helper-sessions/`: helper sessions the build worker started

Transcript copies were taken on 2026-11-22 while the work was still running. Any session still live kept going after the copy.

# auto_experiment: evidence of how I worked with AI

Project: `chaitu0032/auto_experiment`, a master–worker system for running RL experiments. A deterministic Python master observes training telemetry, prunes weak runs, decides the next round and reports to a local dashboard. Workers are Claude Code agents in Herdr panes.

## The AI tools I used and how they fit together

| Tool | What it is | How I used it |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Anthropic's agentic coding CLI | Every agent below is a Claude Code session. I talked to it in plain language in my terminal. |
| **Firstmate** | An open-source supervisor layer for Claude Code | My main session acted as the "first mate": it never edits project code itself. It writes instructions, launches worker agents in isolated git worktrees, watches them, and relays decisions to me. |
| **Second mate** | A persistent Firstmate home with its own charter | I gave auto_experiment its own second mate, so this project's work and records stayed separate from my other work. |
| **Herdr** | A terminal workspace manager for agents | Each worker agent ran in its own visible Herdr tab, so I could watch it or type into it (screenshots 07 and 09). The product I built also uses Herdr panes for its experiment workers. |
| **Lavish editor** | A local review surface for agent-made HTML | I used it to specify requirements and to review the architecture. I accepted, rejected or changed items, wrote comments, and sent structured answers back to the agent (screenshots 01–06). |
| **no-mistakes** | An automated validation pipeline | It reviews, tests, lint-checks and opens the pull request. Its review found real bugs, for example the ASHA pruning-pool gap (screenshots 08 and 09). |

## The workflow, step by step

1. **Asked for requirements, not code.** The first plan was a "thin working slice". I stopped it and asked for the requirements as a Lavish board instead (transcript 02, start).
2. **Requirements round 1, on the Lavish board.**
   - 13 requirements drawn from my own words, plus open questions (screenshot 01).
   - I changed R-02: the master is the brain that decides what to run; workers only execute, and one pane may run several configs (screenshots 02–03).
3. **Requirements round 2.** The agent pointed out a conflict between two of my answers, offered options for the success criteria, and proposed defaults. I said "just build it" on those defaults.
4. **Architecture first, as code.** I asked for the architecture before any implementation, and "as a code and stuff not just prompts". The result was a design document plus a typed Python skeleton, where an LLM may act only behind three validated seams, each with a deterministic fallback (screenshot 06).
5. **Rejected revision 1.** Its dashboard was a 13-line placeholder, and I required a real HTML + JavaScript UI. Revision 2 split the dashboard into a JavaScript frontend and a Python JSON API, and I approved it (screenshot 05). I also caught a component diagram that rendered blank, and it was redrawn.
6. **Implementation and proof.** A worker agent built the system and ran the milestone for real in an isolated Herdr session (screenshot 07):
   - 4 CartPole PPO configurations, with pruning and an LLM decision round
   - a winner verified on 3 seeds
   - human takeover, and recovery after the master was killed outright
7. **Validation.** The no-mistakes review found and fixed issues (screenshot 08). Problems along the way, which I decided how to handle:
   - A committed coverage file with local paths had to be removed from history.
   - The validation tool then deadlocked, and I chose to ship on a fresh branch.
   - An intermittent stop-path test had to be proven to be test timing rather than a race (50-run evidence).
   - The ASHA finding was fixed (screenshot 09).

## Contents

- `screenshots/`: evidence screenshots 01–09 in chronological order. Run `./copy-screenshots.sh` once to fill this folder from the Desktop.
- `transcripts/`: raw, unedited Claude Code session logs (`.jsonl`, one JSON object per line, exactly as Claude Code stored them):
  - `01-main-firstmate-session.jsonl`: my main session with the first mate
  - `02-secondmate-autoexp-session.jsonl`: the auto_experiment second mate (requirements, architecture review, decisions)
  - `03-worker-build-autoexp-v1.jsonl`: the worker that designed, built and proved the system
  - `04-worker-ship-autoexp-ship.jsonl`: the worker that shipped it on the fresh branch and ran validation
  - `05-worker-v1-helper-sessions/`: helper sessions the build worker started

Transcript copies were taken on 2026-11-22 while the work was still running. Any session still live kept going after the copy.

Project: `chaitu0032/auto_experiment`, a master–worker system for running RL experiments. A deterministic Python master observes training telemetry, prunes weak runs, decides the next round and reports to a local dashboard. Workers are Claude Code agents in Herdr panes.

## The AI tools I used and how they fit together

| Tool | What it is | How I used it |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Anthropic's agentic coding CLI | Every agent below is a Claude Code session. I talked to it in plain language in my terminal. |
| **Firstmate** | An open-source supervisor layer for Claude Code | My main session acted as the "first mate": it never edits project code itself. It writes instructions, launches worker agents in isolated git worktrees, watches them, and relays decisions to me. |
| **Second mate** | A persistent Firstmate home with its own charter | I gave auto_experiment its own second mate, so this project's work and records stayed separate from my other work. |
| **Herdr** | A terminal workspace manager for agents | Each worker agent ran in its own visible Herdr tab, so I could watch it or type into it (screenshots 07 and 09). The product I built also uses Herdr panes for its experiment workers. |
| **Lavish editor** | A local review surface for agent-made HTML | I used it to specify requirements and to review the architecture. I accepted, rejected or changed items, wrote comments, and sent structured answers back to the agent (screenshots 01–06). |
| **no-mistakes** | An automated validation pipeline | It reviews, tests, lint-checks and opens the pull request. Its review found real bugs, for example the ASHA pruning-pool gap (screenshots 08 and 09). |

## The workflow, step by step

1. **Asked for requirements, not code.** The first plan was a "thin working slice". I stopped it and asked for the requirements as a Lavish board instead (transcript 02, start).
2. **Requirements round 1, on the Lavish board.**
   - 13 requirements drawn from my own words, plus open questions (screenshot 01).
   - I changed R-02: the master is the brain that decides what to run; workers only execute, and one pane may run several configs (screenshots 02–03).
3. **Requirements round 2.** The agent pointed out a conflict between two of my answers, offered options for the success criteria, and proposed defaults. I said "just build it" on those defaults.
4. **Architecture first, as code.** I asked for the architecture before any implementation, and "as a code and stuff not just prompts". The result was a design document plus a typed Python skeleton, where an LLM may act only behind three validated seams, each with a deterministic fallback (screenshot 06).
5. **Rejected revision 1.** Its dashboard was a 13-line placeholder, and I required a real HTML + JavaScript UI. Revision 2 split the dashboard into a JavaScript frontend and a Python JSON API, and I approved it (screenshot 05). I also caught a component diagram that rendered blank, and it was redrawn.
6. **Implementation and proof.** A worker agent built the system and ran the milestone for real in an isolated Herdr session (screenshot 07):
   - 4 CartPole PPO configurations, with pruning and an LLM decision round
   - a winner verified on 3 seeds
   - human takeover, and recovery after the master was killed outright
7. **Validation.** The no-mistakes review found and fixed issues (screenshot 08). Problems along the way, which I decided how to handle:
   - A committed coverage file with local paths had to be removed from history.
   - The validation tool then deadlocked, and I chose to ship on a fresh branch.
   - An intermittent stop-path test had to be proven to be test timing rather than a race (50-run evidence).
   - The ASHA finding was fixed (screenshot 09).

## Contents

- `screenshots/`: evidence screenshots 01–09 in chronological order. Run `./copy-screenshots.sh` once to fill this folder from the Desktop.
- `transcripts/`: raw, unedited Claude Code session logs (`.jsonl`, one JSON object per line, exactly as Claude Code stored them):
  - `01-main-firstmate-session.jsonl`: my main session with the first mate
  - `02-secondmate-autoexp-session.jsonl`: the auto_experiment second mate (requirements, architecture review, decisions)
  - `03-worker-build-autoexp-v1.jsonl`: the worker that designed, built and proved the system
  - `04-worker-ship-autoexp-ship.jsonl`: the worker that shipped it on the fresh branch and ran validation
  - `05-worker-v1-helper-sessions/`: helper sessions the build worker started

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: ~/.treehouse/firstmate-7bab20/2/firstmate/.claude/skills/ship-landing

# Ship landing

For PR-based ship tasks, the ready signal depends on mode: `no-mistakes` reports `done [at=<epoch>]: PR <url> checks green` after CI is green, while `direct-PR` reports `done [at=<epoch>]: PR <url>` after opening the PR, each only for a non-draft PR; a lane that deliberately holds a draft declares a wait instead, and `bin/fm-pr-check.sh` refuses to arm merge monitoring on a draft.
Run `bin/fm-pr-check.sh <id> <PR url>` with the URL copied from that ready signal or the resolved checks-green `fm-crew-state.sh` line - it records `pr=` and the forge's `pr_head=` when available in the task's meta and arms the watcher's merge poll, which also wakes the supervisor if the ready PR/MR later degrades (failing check, failed head pipeline, merge-train drop) so the worker can be steered to fix it.
With `config/pr-register-scan` present, the watcher can record ready task PRs during its check sweep, including replacing a named PR; see [`docs/configuration.md`](../../../docs/configuration.md#pr-registration-scan-configpr-register-scan) for the full rule. Handle a `check: pr-register:` notification as you would the same result from a manual run.
`bin/fm-dod-lib.sh` owns the named-head gate on that ready signal: a ship `done:` whose named head exists only in the worker's disposable copy is not ready (`bin/fm-crew-state.sh` reports blocked, `bin/fm-pr-check.sh` refuses to register, and a secondmate does not publish that done upstream).
Of those readers only `bin/fm-pr-check.sh` fetches the copy's remotes before it decides, and a no-mistakes pipeline pushes from its own clone, so a no-mistakes ready signal can read blocked until that registration has run: register it before steering.
A refusal that says it could not refresh a remote decided on the last-known refs, so retry it once that remote is reachable.
Otherwise that blocked reading is the gate working, not a stuck worker, so steer the worker on the commit the refusal names rather than waiting.
A `forge=external` task reports `done [at=<epoch>]: review <url> uploaded for review` instead: run `bin/fm-review-check.sh <id> <review url>` rather than `bin/fm-pr-check.sh`, which arms no merge watch, then always escalate the review URL to the captain whatever the yolo setting, because firstmate can neither observe nor perform its approval or merge.
A direct-PR worker pushes that commit to its PR branch, and a local-only worker commits it on its ship branch.
A no-mistakes worker re-validates it with /no-mistakes so the pipeline stays the one publisher; it never pushes from its copy.
In no-mistakes mode the earlier `done [at=<epoch>]: {summary}` is the pipeline handoff and is not gated.
Tell the captain the PR's full `https://...` URL copied from the worker's ready line, the resolved checks-green crew-state line, or the task's `pr=` metadata, a concise outcome summary, and the no-mistakes risk level when applicable.
A captain instruction to merge is explicit authority; `yolo` is the only standing routine merge authority.
For any custom `state/<id>.check.sh` you write yourself, keep it an ordinary single-link mode-`0700` file, print one line only when firstmate should wake, print nothing otherwise, finish before `FM_CHECK_TIMEOUT`, then bind its current bytes with `bin/fm-check-register.sh <id>` before the watcher may execute it.
Retire a custom check only through `bin/fm-check-unregister.sh <id>` (or `bin/fm-teardown.sh` for a spawned task); never hand-compose an `rm` with `$STATE`/`$ID`.

The watcher owns teardown of a merged lane whose merge poll is armed, including a PR merged through `bin/fm-pr-merge.sh`, when the lane is parked or its home has `config/auto-land` ([`docs/configuration.md`](../../../docs/configuration.md#park-on-review)). Otherwise, firstmate tears it down after landing is confirmed.
A lane parked on review (`bin/fm-park.sh`) has no agent and relaunches itself on review activity; `bin/fm-park.sh park <id>` parks one clean lane on request and `bin/fm-park.sh resume <id> --trigger <text>` relaunches one by hand.

Tear down any other ship task only after landing is confirmed.
A teardown refusal for uncommitted or unlanded work is a stop-and-investigate result, never an obstacle to bypass.
Never force teardown without explicit discard authority.
After successful teardown, record completion, retain only the configured recent Done history, and re-evaluate queued work whose blockers and time gates have cleared.

A secondmate is persistent and an empty queue is healthy.
Retire one only on an explicit captain or main-firstmate decision, after loading `secondmate-provisioning`; its home must contain no work under way, and forced discard still requires explicit captain authority.
